rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Turn 3 Game End 4 Cards Overview Play cards to move your Samurai and try to deal 2 damage to your opponent, whilst switching between the Heaven and Earth stances to your advantage Turn First, each player secretly picks a 1st and 2nd card Then reveal both 1st cards and resolve them, before revealing both 2nd cards and resolving them There are two possible stances: Heaven and Earth Movement cards played during Heaven Stance are resolved first Movement cards when in Earth Stance are resolved second A Movement card cannot move one Samurai beyond another, it can still be played but it will at best move the Samurai so they are adjacent instead Attack and Special cards are resolved last If two successful attacks are played, they cancel each other out If only one successful attack is played, it deals damage to the opponent who flips their card to the damaged side After all cards are resolved, card 1 is returned to the hand, whilst card 2 is put aside. In a following round, the same will happen, but the set aside card will return to the hand when the new card 2 is set aside Game End The game ends when a player takes their 2nd damage, they are defeated and the opponent wins! Cards Movement Approach Move 1 space closer Retreat Move 1 space away Charge Move 2 spaces closer Change Stance Change from Heaven to Earth or Earth to Heaven Attack High Strike Only succeeds in Heaven and if the opponent is at 2 spaces away Low Strike Only succeeds in Earth and if the opponent is at 1 space away Balanced Strike Only succeeds if the opponent is at the same location Special Kesa Strike Only succeeds in Heaven and if the opponent is at 0-1 spaces away, then causes you to switch to Earth Zan Tetzu Strike Only succeeds in Earth and if the opponent is at 2-3 spaces away, then causes you to switch to Heaven Counterattack If the opponent lands a successful attack or special attack, deal them back 1 damage

---

In Kiri-ai: The Duel, each player has a hand of cards that represent movements, attacks, or special attacks on the battlefield. At the beginning of each round, each player places two cards from their hand face down next to the battlefield, after which they resolve the actions one card at a time.

With the cards, players advance or retreat in relation to the opponent or strike high or low, attempting to cause damage. Strike your opponent twice in order to win.

[Rating: 1/10] A while ago while commenting on En Garde, I predicted that a minimalist sword-dueling game would just be guessing with no maneuvering. Well, I was correct, this is exactly that. There's a tiny bit of maneuvering, but it doesn't matter because every move becomes a 50/50 guess, both players stuck in a corner. It's just rock paper scissors but you can't repeat the last move, so it's...... less than rock paper scissors. With more components to carry around. [Rating: 2/10] No idea how this is rated a 7.0. This is the most underwhelming 2p game I've ever played. We played on the standard side first to learn the game, and were looking how to play the advanced version, but I stopped a minute into trying to play the advanced version and I just threw it away.   This was awful, I could have someone offer me $20 to take this game from them and I would probably still turn it down. I'd rather play Life: Rivals and that game blows.

[Rating: 3/10] Not as simple as it looks. It's a cool game in a neat little bag that begs to be taken with you anywhere. But you won't be able to teach it quickly or easily to anybody. It's such a headache to even look at let alone understand.

[Rating: 3/10] I thought I would like the micro format with few cards and simultaneous play. Somehow, the two stances and the cards felt clunky and the mind reading never really started in my opinion.

[Rating: 3/10] The concept is good. It's difficult to read the cards, though. And there's very little to explore beyond a tiny game of guessing your opponent's next move.

[Rating: 4/10] Rock-paper-scissors: The Duel.  There just isn't very much here. The card reclamation does leave some room for information and trapping your opponent, but it doesn't feel worth the effort.

[Rating: 4/10] Very simple rock paper scissor tactical game with a bit of memory. Players have symmetrical decks of 6 cards except for 1 special card.  The pros: Very portable, wallet size game.  Easy to teach and requires minimal space to play Fun to fill 10 minutes Card quality is great, they are plastic  The cons: No real depth to it Gets old quickly, we can stand about 3 plays max at one go

[Rating: 4/10] One of those predict what your opponent is gonna do but you don't get to do much predicting... So... Yeah...

[Rating: 4/10] REVIEW: It's true that the game gives you some clues about what cards your opponent might use, but in the end, at most, you can narrow down your opponent's next moves to two or three possible options, and the way to counter each one is so different that you simply have to choose your counterplay at random.  One could argue that you can't ask for much more from a 5-minute game, but if you have that little time, perhaps a board game isn't the best option...
